newsitem.title: USA: Pakistan finances,not politics, led to cut-Moody's.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan finances,not politics, led to cut-Moody's.

text.p: Pakistan's deteriorating financial situation, not this week's political upheaval, prompted Moody's Investors Service to lower the nation's debt ratings on Wednesday, an analyst said.
Moody's reduced Pakistan's foreign currency debt to B2 from B1.
"What led to the downgrade was an ongoing deterioration in the country's financial position that made it much more vulnerable," said David Levey, managing director of sovereign risk at Moody's.
He said Tuesday's ouster of the Bhutto government had not prompted the downgrade, which Moody's first discussed on September 23.
"All of the political elements are still more or less similar to what they had been before," Levey said. "We are just into another interlude between political solutions."
Levey said Pakistan's loss of international reserves and imbalance between assets and liabilities, especially in its short-term debt, made the nation's financial position more fragile.

Moody's also lowered its rating on the country's foreign-currency bank deposits to B3 from B2. It said it may cut this rating further, because this area was the most sensitive to diminished confidence.
Early Tuesday, Pakistani President Farooq Leghari dismissed Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto and formed a caretaker government until February 1997.

Levey said Pakistan's political structure makes it difficult to forge consensus on needed economic reforms. This week's turbulence "does accentuate the pressure for structural (economic) change, but also the resistance to it," he said.

In its release, Moody's noted that Pakistan has made a renewed effort to implement structural economic reforms, as exemplified by the recent renegotiation of an IMF stand-by program from which Pakistan had deviated at midyear.
The IMF agreement would not be affected by the dissolution of the national and provincial governments.

The caretaker government has said it would implement proposed economic measures, which also seem to be supported by the leadership of both major parties, until the new elections can be held in February 1997.

But Moody's said that while the IMF agreement and the government's statements on reform may encourage private capital to flow into the banking system and the equity markets, as well as a rollover of short-term bank credits, Pakistan's financial position has gotten weaker.
